What is Interior Design? Art and Science

Interior design is often misunderstood as merely “decorating,” but it is actually a disciplined practice that combines the art of aesthetics with the science of human behavior and building safety. It involves the planning and execution of interior layouts to maximize space efficiency and improve the quality of life for the inhabitants. The 7 Fundamental Principles of Interior Design

Interior Designer vs. Interior Decorator

While the terms are often used interchangeably, there are distinct differences between an interior designer and an interior decorator. A designer is typically involved in the structural planning and technical aspects of a space, often working alongside architects. A decorator focuses primarily on the surface aesthetics—choosing paint colors, furniture, and fabrics to enhance a room that is already structurally complete. The Core Principles of Interior Design

Achieving a cohesive and inviting aesthetic in your home requires understanding the fundamental principles of interior design. For custom interior designers, these principles guide every decision, from furniture placement to color selection, ensuring a harmonious outcome. These principles are not rigid rules but rather flexible guidelines that help create a balanced and visually appealing space. Our professionals combine these concepts with their creative vision to craft unique interiors tailored to your preferences, ensuring your living room interior design and other spaces reflect your personal style.

  • Balance. This refers to the visual weight of objects, colors, textures, and patterns in a space. It can be symmetrical (identical elements on either side of a central axis) or asymmetrical (different elements with equal visual weight).
  • Harmony. Harmony creates a sense of unity by using similar elements throughout a room, such as consistent color palettes or materials. This ensures all parts of a space work together seamlessly.
  • Rhythm. Rhythm is achieved through repetition, progression, or alternation of elements, guiding the eye smoothly through the space. This can be seen in repeated patterns or varying heights of objects.
  • Emphasis. Every room needs a focal point, something that immediately draws the eye. This could be a fireplace, a piece of art, or a striking piece of furniture. Effective interior design projects always include a well-defined focal point, and exploring different interior color palettes can help establish this.
  • Contrast. Contrast introduces visual interest by juxtaposing different elements, such as light and dark colors, smooth and rough textures, or modern and traditional styles. It prevents a room from looking monotonous.
  • Scale. Scale refers to the size of an object in relation to the room and other objects within it. Proper scale ensures that furniture and decor are neither too large nor too small for the space, preventing it from feeling cramped or empty.
  • Proportion. Proportion is the relationship of parts of an object to the whole and to other objects. It’s about ensuring that all elements in a room feel appropriately sized relative to one another, contributing to overall visual comfort.

Understanding these elements helps in creating an interior that is not only aesthetically pleasing but also functional and comfortable.
